ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure gives an oxygen affinity curve of oxyhemoglobin saturation changing with PO2. The x-axis is PO2 (mmHg), roughly from 0 to 120; the y-axis is Oxyhemoglobin saturation (%), roughly from 0 to 100, and there are horizontal reference lines of 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%. The curve is S-shaped: it is relatively steep in the low PO2 region, and when it rises to about 60 mmHg it is already near the plateau region. According to the rough graph-reading method used in this question, when lung PO2=60 mmHg, the saturation is about 85%; when tissue PO2=20 mmHg, about 20% is taken as the rough/question-intended reading, but by strict visual estimation this curve at 20 mmHg may be slightly higher than 20%. Reasoning: The amount of oxygen obtained by the cells equals the proportion of oxyhemoglobin released during the process of blood going from the lungs to the tissues, that is, the lung saturation minus the saturation still retained at the tissue. Calculating with the rough readings on the graph: 85% - 20% = 65%. Therefore, at cells where PO2=20 mmHg, about 65% of the maximum HbO2 will be released.

method.method_draft: From the graph, blood at PO2 = 60 mmHg is about 85% saturated with oxygen, while at PO2 = 20 mmHg it is about 20% saturated. The amount delivered to cells is the amount lost as blood moves from lungs to tissues: 85% - 20% = 65%. Therefore, 65% of the maximum HbO2 would be delivered.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The figure gives an oxygen affinity curve of oxyhemoglobin saturation changing with PO2. The x-axis is PO2 (mmHg), roughly from 0 to 120; the y-axis is Oxyhemoglobin saturation (%), roughly from 0 to 100, and there are horizontal reference lines of 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100%. The curve is S-shaped: it is relatively steep in the low PO2 region, and when it rises to about 60 mmHg it is already near the plateau region. According to the rough graph-reading method used in this question, when lung PO2=60 mmHg, the saturation is about 85%; when tissue PO2=20 mmHg, about 20% is taken as the rough/question-intended reading, but by strict visual estimation this curve at 20 mmHg may be slightly higher than 20%.

Reasoning: The amount of oxygen obtained by the cells equals the proportion of oxyhemoglobin released during the process of blood going from the lungs to the tissues, that is, the lung saturation minus the saturation still retained at the tissue. Calculating with the rough readings on the graph: 85% - 20% = 65%. Therefore, at cells where PO2=20 mmHg, about 65% of the maximum HbO2 will be released.
